For the most part, we try do deal with any bitwise operations via algebraic reasoning (rewrites over expressions), rather than some bit-blasting approach or something. And I think it's the correct way to do it. Bit-blasting I think makes very little sense for software verification honestly. Most software is not doing bit-level manipulations. And EVM bytecode that comes from the Solidity compiler (and likely other compilers) have very regular structure. So bit-level operations on words are to project out chunks of bits for packed storage slots for the most part. Which can be represented algebraically much cleaner. For example, something like `maxUInt48 &Int (X >>Int 48)` means "give me the second lowest 48 bits" And if that's what you want, then you can just have a rule like `rule maxUInt48 &Int (X >>Int 48) => projectSecondLowest48(X)` Then axiomatize `projectSecondLowest48` directly. Or you can have more generic `project...` functions which can be used. But the point is to take advantage of the structure that the compiler introduces. It's not like it will introduce _arbitrary_ bitwise operation, but highly structured ones. bit-blasting gives up completing on understanding that structure. Here, for example, is the algerbraic presentation of the needed packing/unpacking lemmas for multi-collateral dai: https://github.com/runtimeverification/evm-semantics/blob/master/tests/specs/mcd/word-pack.k So the short answer is "we don't deal with things like shifts directly, we try to handle it at a higher-level, in a Solidity-specific or even contract-specific way"
